expectedText:
TRANSFER-ON-DEATH (TOD) SECURITY REGISTRATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Brokerage, LLC

SECURITY OWNER AND TOD BENEFICIARY DECLARATION
Jordan Alex Lee is the owner of brokerage account ending in 7890 held with Acme Brokerage, LLC. Jordan Alex Lee intends this security or account to be registered in beneficiary form under California's Uniform TOD Security Registration Act, naming Taylor Morgan as TOD beneficiary. If Casey Rivera is also named, Taylor Morgan and Casey Rivera are both named as TOD beneficiaries, to hold as tenants in common if both survive Jordan Alex Lee and the security has not yet been divided between them, unless Acme Brokerage, LLC's own terms and conditions provide otherwise. If Riley Chen is named, Riley Chen is named as a substitute or contingent beneficiary, to take Taylor Morgan's (or Casey Rivera's) share only if that named beneficiary does not survive Jordan Alex Lee. This declaration records Jordan Alex Lee's intended designation for Jordan Alex Lee's own planning purposes; it does not, by itself, register the security or account in beneficiary form. A registration in beneficiary form becomes legally effective only when it is reflected in the registration, account agreement, or other instrument that Acme Brokerage, LLC itself uses to register, open, or modify the security or account.

THE UNIFORM TOD SECURITY REGISTRATION ACT: PURPOSE AND CORE DEFINITIONS
California enacted the Uniform TOD Security Registration Act as Part 3 of Division 5 of the Probate Code (§§ 5500-5512), a nonprobate-transfer statute separate from the Multiple-Party Accounts Law that governs bank accounts and separate from the statute that governs a Transfer-on-Death Deed on real property. Its stated purpose is to let an owner register a security in a title form that transfers the security at death without probate or estate administration, and to protect the entity that implements that title form. Under the Act, a "beneficiary form" is the registration itself — a registration of a security that shows the present owner and the owner's intention about who becomes the owner at the owner's death. A "registering entity" is the person who originates or transfers title to the security by registration, which the statute's own definition says includes a broker maintaining security accounts for customers and a transfer agent or other person acting for or as an issuer of securities. This document addresses a registration of brokerage account ending in 7890 held with Acme Brokerage, LLC in the name of Jordan Alex Lee.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) This part shall be known as and may be cited as the Uniform TOD Security Registration Act.(b) This part shall be liberally construed and applied to promote its underlying purposes and policy.(c) The underlying purposes and policy of this act are to (1) encourage development of a title form for use by individuals that is effective, without probate and estate administration, for transferring property at death in accordance with directions of a deceased owner of a security as included in the title form in which the security is held and (2) protect issuers offering and implementing the new title form."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5500(a)-(c), short title, construction, and stated purpose of the Act (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5500.)
  "(a) “Beneficiary form” means a registration of a security that indicates the present owner of the security and the intention of the owner regarding the person who will become the owner of the security upon the death of the owner."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5501(a), definition of “beneficiary form” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5501.)
  "(c) “Registering entity” means a person who originates or transfers a security title by registration, and includes a broker maintaining security accounts for customers and a transfer agent or other person acting for or as an issuer of securities."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5501(c), definition of “registering entity” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5501.)
  Known gap: This is the Uniform TOD Security Registration Act specifically, codified at Probate Code §§ 5500-5512. It is a distinct statutory scheme from the California Multiple-Party Accounts Law (Part 2 of Division 5, commencing with § 5100, which governs P.O.D. bank accounts and Totten trust accounts) and from the Transfer-on-Death Deed statute (which governs real property); this document does not restate those other schemes. The § 5500(a)-(c) quote below is drawn from three contiguous subdivisions of one statutory section and is treated as one source, not three independent ones; § 5501(a) and § 5501(c) are two separate definitions within the same definitions section and are likewise not independent corroboration of each other. § 5501(b), defining "register" and its derivatives, is not quoted here. This clause states only what the statute's short title, stated purpose, and two of its definitions say; it does not address whether a specific security, account, or instrument actually qualifies for registration in beneficiary form, which depends on the remaining sections of the Act.

WHAT COUNTS AS A “SECURITY” AND A “SECURITY ACCOUNT” — AND THE STATUTE'S OWN LINE AGAINST BANK MULTIPLE-PARTY ACCOUNTS
The Act defines "security" broadly: a share, participation, or other interest in property, in a business, or in an obligation of an enterprise or other issuer, which the statute says includes a certificated security, an uncertificated security, and a security account. "Security account" is itself separately defined, and includes (among other listed categories) a reinvestment account associated with a security, a securities account with a broker, a cash balance in a brokerage account, cash, cash equivalents, and interest, earnings, or dividends earned or declared on a security in such an account — whether or not credited to the account before the owner's death. The statute draws its own express boundary against the bank-account statute covered elsewhere in this document set: § 5501 itself states that it may not be construed to govern cash equivalents in multiple-party accounts that are governed by the California Multiple-Party Accounts Law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(d) “Security” means a share, participation, or other interest in property, in a business, or in an obligation of an enterprise or other issuer, and includes a certificated security, an uncertificated security, and a security account."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5501(d), definition of “security” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5501.)
  "(A) A reinvestment account associated with a security, a securities account with a broker, a cash balance in a brokerage account, cash, cash equivalents, interest, earnings, or dividends earned or declared on a security in an account, a reinvestment account, or a brokerage account, whether or not credited to the account before the owner’s death."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5501(e)(1)(A), one category within the definition of “security account” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5501.)
  "This section may not be construed to govern cash equivalents in multiple-party accounts that are governed by the California Multiple-Party Accounts Law, Part 2 (commencing with Section 5100)."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5501(f), express carve-out for cash equivalents governed by the Multiple-Party Accounts Law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5501.)
  Known gap: Only subdivision (e)(1)(A) of the "security account" definition is quoted below; subdivisions (e)(1)(B) (investment management and custody accounts with a trust company or bank trust department) and (e)(1)(C) (replacement or product cash balances), and the separate (e)(2) definition of "cash equivalent," are part of the same statutory definition but are not independently quoted here. The § 5501(f) boundary against the Multiple-Party Accounts Law is narrow on its own terms — it excludes only "cash equivalents in multiple-party accounts," not every brokerage or investment account outright — so this clause does not resolve which statute governs a specific account that could plausibly be described under either scheme; that determination depends on how a specific account is actually titled and structured with the financial institution or registering entity holding it.

WHO MAY REGISTER IN BENEFICIARY FORM, AND WHICH STATE'S LAW APPLIES
Only individuals may obtain a registration in beneficiary form — sole ownership by one individual, or multiple ownership by two or more individuals holding with right of survivorship rather than as tenants in common. The statute's own text states that multiple owners of a security registered in beneficiary form hold as joint tenants with right of survivorship, as tenants by the entireties, or as owners of community property held in survivorship form, and not as tenants in common. Separately, the Act sets out which jurisdiction's law can authorize a beneficiary-form registration: California's version applies if the form is authorized by this or a similar statute of the state where the issuer or registering entity is organized, where the registering entity's principal office or transfer-agent office is located, where the registration is made, or of the state listed as Jordan Alex Lee's address at the time of registration.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Only individuals whose registration of a security shows sole ownership by one individual or multiple ownership by two or more individuals with right of survivorship, rather than as tenants in common, may obtain registration in beneficiary form. Multiple owners of a security registered in beneficiary form hold as joint tenants with right of survivorship, as tenants by the entireties, or as owners of community property held in survivorship form, and not as tenants in common."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5502, eligible owners and the forms in which multiple owners hold (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5502.)
  "A security may be registered in beneficiary form if the form is authorized by this or a similar statute of the state of organization of the issuer or registering entity, the location of the registering entity’s principal office, the office of its transfer agent or its office making the registration, or by this or a similar statute of the law of the state listed as the owner’s address at the time of registration. A registration governed by the law of a jurisdiction in which this or similar legislation is not in force or was not in force when a registration in beneficiary form was made is nevertheless presumed to be valid and authorized as a matter of contract law."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5503, which jurisdiction's law can authorize the registration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5503.)
  Known gap: The statutory text of § 5502 lists "tenants by the entireties" as one of the three forms in which multiple owners hold a security registered in beneficiary form. California does not generally recognize tenancy by the entirety as a form of concurrent ownership between spouses (unlike some other states) — this appears to be uniform-act language carried into the California statute without adaptation, and this document does not resolve what legal effect, if any, that listed form would have for California owners. Separately, § 5503's final sentence — that a registration is "presumed to be valid" even under the law of a jurisdiction where no similar TOD-security statute is or was in force — is a presumption, not a guarantee, and this document does not resolve how that presumption would be rebutted in a specific jurisdiction or dispute.

HOW A REGISTRATION IN BENEFICIARY FORM IS CREATED, AND THE “TOD” / “POD” LABELS
A security — whether evidenced by a certificate or held in an account — is registered in beneficiary form when the registration includes a designation of a beneficiary to take ownership at the death of the owner, or at the death of the last survivor of multiple owners. The statute specifies how that designation may be shown: by the words "transfer on death" or the abbreviation "TOD," or by the words "pay on death" or the abbreviation "POD," placed after the name of the registered owner and before the name of the beneficiary.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A security, whether evidenced by certificate or account, is registered in beneficiary form when the registration includes a designation of a beneficiary to take the ownership at the death of the owner or the deaths of all multiple owners."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5504, when a security is registered in beneficiary form (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5504.)
  "Registration in beneficiary form may be shown by the words “transfer on death” or the abbreviation “TOD,” or by the words “pay on death” or the abbreviation “POD,” after the name of the registered owner and before the name of a beneficiary."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5505, the “TOD” and “POD” wording that shows the designation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5505.)
  Known gap: These two sections state only what wording shows a beneficiary-form registration; they do not themselves address the account-opening or reregistration paperwork through which a registering entity actually implements a TOD or POD designation — that is addressed in a separate clause of this document describing a registering entity's own terms and conditions. The identical "TOD" and "POD" abbreviations are also used under California's separate Transfer-on-Death Deed statute (for real property) and its Multiple-Party Accounts Law (for bank accounts); this clause addresses only the security-registration meaning of those abbreviations under Probate Code § 5505, not their use under those other, separately governed statutes.

NO EFFECT UNTIL DEATH, AND FREE REVOCABILITY BY THE OWNER
A TOD beneficiary designation on a registration in beneficiary form has no effect on ownership of brokerage account ending in 7890 until Jordan Alex Lee's death. Until then, the registration may be canceled or changed at any time by the sole owner, or by all then-surviving owners if there is more than one, and the statute states this can be done without the consent of Taylor Morgan or any other named beneficiary.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The designation of a TOD beneficiary on a registration in beneficiary form has no effect on ownership until the owner’s death. A registration of a security in beneficiary form may be canceled or changed at any time by the sole owner or all then surviving owners without the consent of the beneficiary."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5506, no effect on ownership until death, and revocability without beneficiary consent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5506.)
  Known gap: This single statutory section (§ 5506) does not itself specify the mechanical steps or paperwork by which an owner would cancel or change a registration — those mechanics are set by the registering entity's own terms and conditions under a separate section of the Act, addressed elsewhere in this document. The statute also requires that all then-surviving owners agree to a change where a security is jointly owned; it does not itself address what happens if surviving co-owners disagree, or supply a mechanism to resolve such a disagreement.

EFFECT AT THE OWNER'S DEATH: PASSAGE TO SURVIVING BENEFICIARIES, TENANCY IN COMMON AMONG MULTIPLE BENEFICIARIES, AND LAPSE TO THE ESTATE
On the death of a sole owner, or the death of the last survivor of multiple owners, ownership of a security registered in beneficiary form passes to the beneficiary or beneficiaries who survive all the owners. On proof of the owners' deaths and compliance with the registering entity's own applicable requirements, the security may be reregistered in the surviving beneficiary's or beneficiaries' names. If more than one beneficiary survives, the statute states that — until the security is divided — those beneficiaries hold their interests as tenants in common. If no beneficiary survives the death of all owners, the statute directs that the security belongs to the estate of the deceased sole owner, or the estate of the last owner to die.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "On death of a sole owner or the last to die of all multiple owners, ownership of securities registered in beneficiary form passes to the beneficiary or beneficiaries who survive all owners. On proof of death of all owners and compliance with any applicable requirements of the registering entity, a security registered in beneficiary form may be reregistered in the name of the beneficiary or beneficiaries who survive the death of all owners. Until division of the security after the death of all owners, multiple beneficiaries surviving the death of all owners hold their interests as tenants in common. If no beneficiary survives the death of all owners, the security belongs to the estate of the deceased sole owner or the estate of the last to die of all multiple owners."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5507, passage of ownership at death, tenancy in common among survivors, and lapse to the estate (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5507.)
  Known gap: This single statutory section (§ 5507) states the default outcomes at death; it does not itself define what counts as "surviving" the owner for these purposes — for example, it does not set out a required survival period comparable to the 120-hour rule found in California's Uniform Simultaneous Death Act, which is addressed elsewhere in this document set as a separate statutory scheme, not part of this Act's own text. It also does not address the registering entity's own documentation requirements for "proof of death," which the Act leaves to that entity's terms and conditions.

THE REGISTERING ENTITY'S DISCRETION TO OFFER TOD REGISTRATION, AND ITS DISCHARGE FROM CLAIMS AFTER A GOOD-FAITH TRANSFER
Acme Brokerage, LLC is not statutorily required to offer or accept a request for security registration in beneficiary form. If it does offer registration in beneficiary form, the statute treats the owner requesting it as assenting to the protections the Act gives to the registering entity. Once a registering entity registers a transfer under the death-transfer section described elsewhere in this document, and does so in good-faith reliance on the registration itself, on the Act, and on information such as an affidavit of the deceased owner's personal representative or information from the surviving beneficiary, the statute discharges the registering entity from all claims to the security by the deceased owner's estate, creditors, heirs, or devisees. That statutory protection does not extend to a reregistration or payment made after the registering entity has received written notice from any claimant objecting to implementation of the beneficiary-form registration.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) A registering entity is not required to offer or to accept requests for security registration in beneficiary form. If a registration in beneficiary form is offered by a registering entity, the owner requesting registration in beneficiary form assents to the protections given to the registering entity by this part."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5508(a), no statutory requirement to offer beneficiary-form registration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5508.)
  "(c) A registering entity is discharged from all claims to a security by the estate, creditors, heirs, or devisees of a deceased owner if it registers a transfer of the security in accordance with Section 5507 and does so in good faith reliance (1) on the registration, (2) on this part, and (3) on information provided to it by affidavit of the personal representative of the deceased owner, or by the surviving beneficiary or the surviving beneficiary’s representatives, or other information available to the registering entity. The protections of this part do not extend to a reregistration or payment made after a registering entity has received written notice from any claimant to any interest in the security objecting to implementation of a registration in beneficiary form. No other notice or other information available to the registering entity shall affect its right to protection under this part."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5508(c), discharge from claims after a good-faith transfer, and the written-notice exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5508.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes § 5508(a) and § 5508(c); it does not separately quote § 5508(b) (the registering entity's agreement to implement a registration it accepts) or § 5508(d), which states that the registering entity's own protection from claims does not affect the rights of beneficiaries in disputes between themselves and other claimants over the security, its value, or its proceeds — in other words, this discharge protects the registering entity as an institution, but does not itself resolve a dispute among people claiming the security or its proceeds.

NONTESTAMENTARY CHARACTER OF THE TRANSFER, AND PRESERVATION OF SURVIVING-SPOUSE, CREDITOR, AND COMMUNITY-PROPERTY RIGHTS
The statute characterizes a transfer on death resulting from a registration in beneficiary form as effective by reason of the contract between the owner and the registering entity and the Act itself — and states that it is "not testamentary." The Act also states, in the same section, that it does not limit the rights of a surviving spouse or of creditors of a security owner against beneficiaries and other transferees under other California law. Separately, the Act states that nothing in it alters the community character of community property or community rights in community property, and that it is subject to a separate chapter of the Probate Code (Chapter 2, commencing with § 5010, of Part 1 of Division 5).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) Any transfer on death resulting from a registration in beneficiary form is effective by reason of the contract regarding the registration between the owner and the registering entity and this part and is not testamentary.(b) This part does not limit the rights of a surviving spouse or creditors of security owners against beneficiaries and other transferees under other laws of this state."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5509, nontestamentary character, and preservation of surviving-spouse and creditor rights (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5509.)
  "Nothing in this part alters the community character of community property or community rights in community property. This part is subject to Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 5010) of Part 1 of Division 5."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5511, no alteration of community property character; cross-reference to Chapter 2 of Part 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5511.)
  Known gap: "Not testamentary" describes how the transfer takes legal effect — by contract and statute rather than as a testamentary disposition subject to the Probate Code's will-execution formalities — and this document does not otherwise restate what those will-execution formalities require. § 5509(b)'s preservation of surviving-spouse and creditor rights "under other laws of this state" does not itself identify what those other laws provide or how a specific spouse's or creditor's claim would be resolved against a specific beneficiary. § 5511's cross-reference to Chapter 2 (commencing with § 5010) of Part 1 of Division 5 is quoted here only as a cross-reference; this document does not independently fetch, quote, or verify the text of that other chapter, and does not represent what it provides beyond what § 5511 itself says.

THE REGISTERING ENTITY'S OWN TERMS AND CONDITIONS, SUBSTITUTED (“LDPS”) BENEFICIARIES, AND WHEN THIS ACT APPLIES
A registering entity that offers to accept registrations in beneficiary form may establish its own terms and conditions for receiving requests for registration and for implementing them, including requests to cancel a previously registered TOD designation or to reregister for a change of beneficiary. Among other things the statute permits those terms and conditions to address, the Act specifically recognizes a way to name a substitute beneficiary: appending the letters "LDPS" (for "lineal descendants per stirpes") to the name of the primary beneficiary. That designation substitutes the named beneficiary's descendants, if the beneficiary does not survive the owner, with those descendants identified and sharing according to the law of the beneficiary's domicile at the owner's death governing inheritance by descendants of an intestate. Separately, the Act states its own applicability: it applies to registrations of securities in beneficiary form made before, on, or after January 1, 1999, by decedents dying on or after January 1, 1999.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) A registering entity offering to accept registrations in beneficiary form may establish the terms and conditions under which it will receive requests for (1) registrations in beneficiary form, and (2) implementation of registrations in beneficiary form, including requests for cancellation of previously registered TOD beneficiary designations and requests for reregistration to effect a change of beneficiary."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5510(a), registering entity's authority to set its own terms and conditions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5510.)
  "Substitution may be indicated by appending to the name of the primary beneficiary the letters LDPS, standing for “lineal descendants per stirpes.” This designation substitutes a deceased beneficiary’s descendants who survive the owner for a beneficiary who fails to so survive, the descendants to be identified and to share in accordance with the law of the beneficiary’s domicile at the owner’s death governing inheritance by descendants of an intestate."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5510(b), the “LDPS” substitute-beneficiary designation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5510.)
  "This part applies to registrations of securities in beneficiary form made before, on, or after January 1, 1999, by decedents dying on or after January 1, 1999."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5512, applicability of the Act by registration and date-of-death (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5512.)
  Known gap: § 5510(b)'s LDPS mechanism determines a substitute beneficiary's shares by reference to "the law of the beneficiary's domicile at the owner's death" — a law that could be a jurisdiction other than California depending on where the named beneficiary was domiciled, and that this document does not independently identify or apply. § 5510(a) is quoted only as to a registering entity's authority to set terms and conditions; the statute's own illustrative registration formats in § 5510(c) (for example, "John S. Brown TOD John S. Brown, Jr.") are the statute's own examples of formats a registering entity may authorize, not a representation that any specific brokerage firm or transfer agent uses that exact format. § 5512's applicability rule means that a decedent who died before January 1, 1999 is not covered by this Act regardless of when a beneficiary-form registration was made.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
SIGNATURE AND DATE: Jordan Alex Lee signs and dates this declaration below.

Signature of Jordan Alex Lee: _________________________ Date: _______________

Printed name: _________________________

ACKNOWLEDGMENT: Jordan Alex Lee understands that this declaration is a planning worksheet reflecting Jordan Alex Lee's intended TOD beneficiary designation for brokerage account ending in 7890 at Acme Brokerage, LLC, and that it does not itself register, open, or modify any security or account. Jordan Alex Lee understands that to make the designation legally effective, Jordan Alex Lee must separately complete Acme Brokerage, LLC's own registration, beneficiary form, or account agreement naming Taylor Morgan (and Casey Rivera and Riley Chen, if applicable) as TOD or POD beneficiary, and that Acme Brokerage, LLC may require government-issued identification, an original signature, or additional paperwork of its own choosing before doing so, and is not required by statute to offer this form of registration at all. Jordan Alex Lee further understands that the designation can generally be canceled or changed at any time before Jordan Alex Lee's death — by Jordan Alex Lee alone if sole owner, or by all then-surviving owners if jointly owned — without Taylor Morgan's consent, and that it has no effect on ownership until Jordan Alex Lee's death.

NOTARIZATION NOTICE: California's Uniform TOD Security Registration Act does not require this declaration to be notarized or witnessed to be effective; what governs is the registration or account agreement actually on file with Acme Brokerage, LLC. This declaration is kept for Jordan Alex Lee's own records, alongside a copy of the TOD or POD registration paperwork Acme Brokerage, LLC provides.

The statute specifies how that designation may be shown: by the words "transfer on death" or the abbreviation "TOD," or by the words "pay on death" or the abbreviation "POD," placed after the name of the registered owner and before the name of the beneficiary.

citations.cite: when a security is registered in beneficiary form
citations.quote: A security, whether evidenced by certificate or account, is registered in beneficiary form when the registration includes a designation of a beneficiary to take the ownership at the death of the owner or the deaths of all multiple owners.

citations.cite: the “TOD” and “POD” wording that shows the designation
citations.quote: Registration in beneficiary form may be shown by the words “transfer on death” or the abbreviation “TOD,” or by the words “pay on death” or the abbreviation “POD,” after the name of the registered owner and before the name of a beneficiary.

expectedJSON.gap: These two sections state only what wording shows a beneficiary-form registration; they do not themselves address the account-opening or reregistration paperwork through which a registering entity actually implements a TOD or POD designation — that is addressed in a separate clause of this document describing a registering entity's own terms and conditions. The identical "TOD" and "POD" abbreviations are also used under California's separate Transfer-on-Death Deed statute (for real property) and its Multiple-Party Accounts Law (for bank accounts); this clause addresses only the security-registration meaning of those abbreviations under Probate Code § 5505, not their use under those other, separately governed statutes.

expectedJSON.body: On the death of a sole owner, or the death of the last survivor of multiple owners, ownership of a security registered in beneficiary form passes to the beneficiary or beneficiaries who survive all the owners. On proof of the owners' deaths and compliance with the registering entity's own applicable requirements, the security may be reregistered in the surviving beneficiary's or beneficiaries' names. If more than one beneficiary survives, the statute states that — until the security is divided — those beneficiaries hold their interests as tenants in common. If no beneficiary survives the death of all owners, the statute directs that the security belongs to the estate of the deceased sole owner, or the estate of the last owner to die.

citations.cite: passage of ownership at death, tenancy in common among survivors, and lapse to the estate
citations.quote: On death of a sole owner or the last to die of all multiple owners, ownership of securities registered in beneficiary form passes to the beneficiary or beneficiaries who survive all owners. On proof of death of all owners and compliance with any applicable requirements of the registering entity, a security registered in beneficiary form may be reregistered in the name of the beneficiary or beneficiaries who survive the death of all owners. Until division of the security after the death of all owners, multiple beneficiaries surviving the death of all owners hold their interests as tenants in common. If no beneficiary survives the death of all owners, the security belongs to the estate of the deceased sole owner or the estate of the last to die of all multiple owners.

expectedJSON.body: A registering entity that offers to accept registrations in beneficiary form may establish its own terms and conditions for receiving requests for registration and for implementing them, including requests to cancel a previously registered TOD designation or to reregister for a change of beneficiary. Among other things the statute permits those terms and conditions to address, the Act specifically recognizes a way to name a substitute beneficiary: appending the letters "LDPS" (for "lineal descendants per stirpes") to the name of the primary beneficiary. That designation substitutes the named beneficiary's descendants, if the beneficiary does not survive the owner, with those descendants identified and sharing according to the law of the beneficiary's domicile at the owner's death governing inheritance by descendants of an intestate. Separately, the Act states its own applicability: it applies to registrations of securities in beneficiary form made before, on, or after January 1, 1999, by decedents dying on or after January 1, 1999.

citations.cite: registering entity's authority to set its own terms and conditions
citations.quote: (a) A registering entity offering to accept registrations in beneficiary form may establish the terms and conditions under which it will receive requests for (1) registrations in beneficiary form, and (2) implementation of registrations in beneficiary form, including requests for cancellation of previously registered TOD beneficiary designations and requests for reregistration to effect a change of beneficiary.

Substitution may be indicated by appending to the name of the primary beneficiary the letters LDPS, standing for “lineal descendants per stirpes.” This designation substitutes a deceased beneficiary’s descendants who survive the owner for a beneficiary who fails to so survive, the descendants to be identified and to share in accordance with the law of the beneficiary’s domicile at the owner’s death governing inheritance by descendants of an intestate.

citations.cite: applicability of the Act by registration and date-of-death
citations.quote: This part applies to registrations of securities in beneficiary form made before, on, or after January 1, 1999, by decedents dying on or after January 1, 1999.

expectedJSON.gap: § 5510(b)'s LDPS mechanism determines a substitute beneficiary's shares by reference to "the law of the beneficiary's domicile at the owner's death" — a law that could be a jurisdiction other than California depending on where the named beneficiary was domiciled, and that this document does not independently identify or apply. § 5510(a) is quoted only as to a registering entity's authority to set terms and conditions; the statute's own illustrative registration formats in § 5510(c) (for example, "John S. Brown TOD John S. Brown, Jr.") are the statute's own examples of formats a registering entity may authorize, not a representation that any specific brokerage firm or transfer agent uses that exact format. § 5512's applicability rule means that a decedent who died before January 1, 1999 is not covered by this Act regardless of when a beneficiary-form registration was made.
